title: Ethnicity‐ and gender‐based social stressors and parental socialization in Korean Chinese adolescent adjustment
abstract: Abstract Although extensive research has documented the adverse effects of social stressors, such as ethnicity‐ and gender‐based discrimination, on adolescent development, much of this work has focused on Western contexts. This survey study was conducted with 267 Korean Chinese adolescents (59% female; M age = 15.24 years, SD age = 1.66, age range: 12–18 years), examining how three forms of perceived discrimination linked to adolescents' psychosocial and academic adjustment, as well as the roles of parental socialization practices. Perceived discrimination by South Koreans, but not by Han Chinese, was linked to more depressive symptoms and delinquency. Gender nonconformity teasing was associated with more depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation. Parental cultural socialization was associated with lower suicidal ideation and delinquency and higher school attachment. Parental gender norm socialization was positively associated with school attachment. These findings underscore the negative implications of ethnicity‐ and gender‐based discrimination, highlight the positive developmental correlates of parental cultural socialization, and suggest that parental gender norm socialization might serve a context‐specific adaptive function.
